src/content/atlas.ts: Thousands of flamingos winter on Sebkhet Sijoumi, a salt lagoon inside Tunis itself.
The lagoons of Korba on Cap Bon are a wetland reserve where flamingos feed, and where a colony has nested.
Lake Ichkeul is a winter home for ducks, geese and coots that fly in from Europe.
White storks nest on pylons, roofs and the old railway station of Sejnane, and across the Medjerda valley.
Africa’s only native deer lives in the oak forests of El Feija National Park, where it was brought back from the edge of extinction.
Wild boar are common in the cork-oak forests of the Kroumirie mountains.
In spring, birds of prey gather over El Haouaria before crossing the sea to Sicily; the town has kept its tradition of falconry.
The Kuriat Islands off Monastir are Tunisia’s main nesting beach for loggerhead sea turtles, watched over each summer since 1997.
Once extinct in the wild, this desert antelope was brought back to Bou Hedma in 1985 and now lives in several southern parks.
Around Douz, dromedaries are still raised, raced at the Festival of the Sahara, and ridden into the dunes.
The small desert fox with huge ears lives in the sands of the Grand Erg Oriental and comes out at night.
Ferries from La Goulette to Marseille, Genoa and Sicily
src/content/el-jem.ts: El Jem, Mahdia governorate. About 200 km south of Tunis and 65 km from Sousse.
Trains on the Tunis–Sfax line stop in El Jem; the station is a short walk from the amphitheatre. By car, take the A1 motorway.
Spring and autumn; arrive early or late afternoon for soft light. In summer the El Jem symphonic music festival is held inside the amphitheatre.
The El Jem archaeological museum, with Roman mosaics from the villas of Thysdrus.
Check current opening hours and prices before you go; the ticket usually includes the museum.
The outer wall is ringed by 64 arches on each of three levels, framed by Corinthian and composite half-columns. A fourth, solid level (the attic) once crowned the top; only fragments survive.
Roman Thysdrus grew rich on olive oil exported across the Mediterranean. In 238 CE a revolt here proclaimed the local governor Gordian I emperor. This was the third amphitheatre built on the site.
Two concentric rings of arches form vaulted corridors on every level. They let tens of thousands of people reach their seats, and leave the amphitheatre, in minutes.
Look closely at the blocks: visitors have left their mark for centuries. You can find carvings dated 1914 and a soldier’s "1943", from the Second World War campaign in Tunisia.
The sand floor (64 × 39 m) hosted gladiator fights and wild-animal hunts with lions, leopards and bears brought from Africa’s interior. The high podium wall protected the crowd.

Two underground galleries cross beneath the arena. Animals, fighters and stage machinery waited in the vaulted cells, then rose through trapdoors into the light. Today a glass roof covers the central slot.
The main gallery continues as a long barrel-vaulted tunnel under the seats, so animals and performers could be moved in without crossing the crowd.
Around 30,000–35,000 spectators sat here, ranked by status: officials nearest the arena, ordinary citizens higher up. The lower tiers you see were restored; the upper ones collapsed long ago.
Every summer the amphitheatre becomes a concert hall for the International Symphonic Music Festival of El Jem. Orchestras play where gladiators once fought.
From the top gallery you look over the modern town. For centuries its houses, and even the Great Mosque of Kairouan, were partly built with stone taken from the amphitheatre.
The amphitheatre was used as a fortress more than once. In 1695 breaches were opened in the wall so it could no longer shelter rebels, and the gap was never rebuilt.
Local tradition says the Berber queen Dihya, known as the Kahena, held out here against the Arab armies at the end of the 7th century. Historians debate it, but the story is still told in El Jem.
src/content/guide.ts: Medina Festival of Tunis

Evening concerts of traditional and tarab music, theatre and workshops in the old town of Tunis during Ramadan; the 42nd edition was in 2026. It follows Ramadan, so it comes about eleven days earlier each year.
Festival of the Saharan Ksour

A spring festival of southern Berber heritage, founded in 1979: folk shows, horsemanship and a crafts fair around the fortified granaries. It has been irregular: it paused after 2022, and a revival was announced for March 2026.
Ghriba pilgrimage

The yearly Jewish pilgrimage to the El Ghriba synagogue on Djerba, around Lag BaOmer, with prayers and processions. Its date follows the Hebrew calendar; it has been smaller since 2023 and is held under tight security.
Falconry Festival of El Haouaria
Three days on Cap Bon where local falconers show and compete with trained sparrowhawks and falcons. Held each June; 2025 was the 56th edition.
Tabarka Jazz Festival
Jazz, world and contemporary music on the north coast since 1973, with free street jazz in the evenings. It came back in July 2026 after a six-year break, so it is not held every year.
Dougga Festival
Summer concerts in the Roman theatre of Dougga, mostly Tunisian artists. Held most summers; the 50th edition ran over ten evenings in July 2026.
Malouf Festival of Testour
A week of malouf, the Arab-Andalusian music of Tunisia, in the Andalusian town of Testour, since 1967. Usually in July, but the 2026 edition was cancelled.
Aoussou Carnival
Sousse’s summer carnival: floats, brass bands and folk troupes from Tunisia and abroad, traditionally on 24 July near Boujaafar beach.
International Festival of Carthage
Tunisia’s best-known summer festival, every July and August since 1964 in the Roman theatre of Carthage: concerts by Arab and international artists, some theatre and dance.
Hammamet International Festival
Music and stage shows since 1964 in an open-air amphitheatre of 1,000 seats above the Gulf of Hammamet, through July and August.
El Jem Symphonic Music Festival
Orchestras from Tunisia and abroad play inside the Roman amphitheatre of El Jem, every summer since the mid-1980s.
Sfax International Festival
Concerts, shows and films in the open-air theatre of Sfax, from late July to mid-August; 2026 was the 46th edition.
Kerkennah Festival
A popular summer festival on the Kerkennah islands: music, comedy, rap and shows for children. The 30th edition was in summer 2025.
Mouled in Kairouan
Hundreds of thousands come to Kairouan for the Prophet’s birthday, with free shows and light displays over about a week. It follows the Islamic calendar: late August in 2026, then earlier each year.
Carthage Theatre Days
A theatre festival since 1983, with more than 80 shows from Tunisia, the Arab world and Africa, mostly at the City of Culture in Tunis. Recent editions were in late November.
Carthage Film Festival
African and Arab cinema in Tunis since 1966, with the Tanit d’or award. Traditionally October–November; recent editions were in December.
International Festival of the Sahara
Four days of desert life at the end of December in Douz: camel races, horsemanship, a Bedouin wedding, poetry and music, at the edge of the dunes.
Festival of the Oases
Late December in Tozeur, first held in 1938: the oases and the date harvest, with concerts, horsemanship, street arts and date markets.
3 days: Tunis and Roman Africa
A long weekend from Tunis, no hotel change needed.
The medina of Tunis in the morning, the mosaics of the Bardo in the afternoon.
The ruins of Carthage by the sea, then sunset in the blue and white village of Sidi Bou Said.
A day trip to Dougga, the best-kept Roman town in Africa, about two hours from Tunis.
7 days: monuments and beaches
The great monuments of the north and centre, with time on the beach.
The medina of Tunis and the Bardo museum.
Carthage and Sidi Bou Said.
Drive to Kairouan: the Great Mosque, the Aghlabid basins and the makroudh bakeries.
The amphitheatre of El Jem in the morning, then the sea at Mahdia.
A beach day at Mahdia, with clear water and the old town on its cape.
The ribats of Monastir and Sousse, and the medina of Sousse.
Hammamet: the medina by the beach, about an hour from Tunis airport.
10 days: from Carthage to the Sahara
The whole country, north to south. Fly home from Djerba to save the drive back.
Kairouan, the holy city.
The long drive to the oasis of Tozeur, its palm groves and its old quarter of patterned brick.
The mountain oasis of Chebika, then sunset at the rocks of Ong Jemel.
Across the salt lake of Chott el Djerid to Douz, the gate of the Sahara.
A night at Ksar Ghilane, among the dunes, with a warm spring to bathe in.
The cave houses of Matmata.
The Berber village of Chenini and the granaries of Ksar Ouled Soltane, then on to Djerba.
Djerba: Houmt Souk, the Ghriba synagogue and a last swim.

Called kosksi at home: semolina steamed over a stew, served with vegetables and meat or fish that change with the region and the season. Its know-how is on the UNESCO list of intangible heritage since 2020, shared with Algeria, Mauritania and Morocco.
A paper-thin sheet of malsouka pastry folded around a filling and fried until crisp. The classic hides a whole egg with tuna, onion, parsley and harissa.
Chickpeas in a garlic and cumin broth over pieces of bread, topped with harissa, olive oil, egg, capers or tuna. Once a winter breakfast, now eaten at any hour.
Eggs cooked in a spicy sauce of tomatoes, green chillies and harissa, often with merguez sausage. Mop it up with bread.
Kairouan and Tunis, each with its own recipe
Fried peppers and tomatoes chopped together with eggs, eaten by dipping bread. Kairouan’s is very spicy; the Tunis one adds pumpkin.
Cap Bon, above all Nabeul
Tunisia’s chilli paste: sun-dried peppers ground with salt, garlic and coriander. It seasons everyday food and is on the UNESCO list of intangible heritage since 2022.
A dark green sauce of powdered mulukhiyah leaves slowly cooked in olive oil with beef or lamb, eaten with bread.
Small diamonds of semolina filled with dates. They come from Kairouan, which held the first national makroudh festival in 2008.
Sidi Bou Said
A fried doughnut dusted with sugar or soaked in honey. Sidi Bou Said is famous for it.
Sweet mint tea poured over pine nuts in the glass; almonds or peanuts sometimes take their place.
A small fried roll filled with tuna, egg, potato, olives, capers, preserved lemon and harissa: the classic street snack.
Its name means “mixed”: a stew of tomatoes, peppers, onions and garlic, often with eggs.
The oases of the Djerid and Nefzaoua
Soft, honey-sweet dates, the “dates of light”, grown in the desert oases. They also fill the makroudh.
Olive oil is central to life around Sfax, which makes about 40% of Tunisia’s. The geographer al-Idrisi praised its olives in the 12th century.

Visas and passports
No visa for up to 90 days for most of the EU, the UK, the US, Canada, Switzerland, Norway, Russia, China, the Gulf states, Algeria, Libya and Morocco.
Ukrainians normally need a visa, except on an organised tour with a hotel voucher.
Bring your passport: identity cards are not accepted. The UK asks for a passport valid for the whole stay; Canada advises six months beyond departure.
Officers may ask for a return ticket and where you are staying. There is no e-visa: a visa, when needed, comes from a Tunisian embassy.
Rules change and depend on your nationality: check with the Tunisian embassy before booking.
Money
The dinar (TND) is a closed currency: you cannot bring dinars in or take them out. Change money after you land.
Change at banks, licensed exchange offices, hotels or post offices, with your passport. Keep the receipts: you need them to change dinars back before you leave.
Cash machines are common in towns and take Visa and Mastercard. Many hotels and restaurants take cards; taxis, louages, markets and small places want cash.
Hotels charge a small tourist tax per person and night, for up to ten nights.
Safety
Most visits are trouble-free, but the UK, US and Canadian governments ask travellers to stay alert to the risk of terrorism, at tourist and religious sites and in crowds.
Theft is the most common crime: keep valuables out of sight. Avoid demonstrations, and carry a copy of your passport.
Drones need a permit. Follow the flags on the beach.
Health
Tap water is treated in the cities and on the coast; bottled water is cheap and wiser in the countryside and the south.
Ask a travel clinic about hepatitis A and typhoid. Take insurance that covers treatment and repatriation: clinics expect payment on the spot.
Pharmacies are common in towns. Bring your medicines in their boxes with a doctor’s note.
Inland summers are very hot: drink often, cover up and rest at midday. Do not touch stray dogs; get care at once after a bite.
Emergency numbers
Police: 197. National Guard (countryside): 193.
Ambulance: 190. Fire and road accidents: 198.
For a lost passport, call your embassy in Tunis.
Phone and internet
Three networks: Ooredoo, Orange and Tunisie Telecom, with counters in the arrivals hall of Tunis–Carthage. A SIM needs your passport itself, not a copy.
A travel eSIM can be set up before you leave. Hotels and cafés in towns usually have Wi-Fi.
The country code is +216, then eight digits.
Electricity
230 V, 50 Hz, with two round pins (types C and E): a continental European plug fits.
Summer heat can cause short power cuts.
From the airport
Tunis–Carthage: bus 635 to Tunis Marine every 30–40 minutes by day, cash on board; or a yellow taxi with the meter on. Ride apps work too.
Enfidha–Hammamet: no train. Agree the taxi fare before you set off; package holidays usually include the transfer.
Monastir: the Sahel Metro stops 150 m from the terminal, with trains to Monastir, Sousse and Mahdia.
Djerba: taxis to Houmt Souk and the hotels; ask for the meter.
Getting around
Louages are shared minibuses between towns. They leave when full, at fixed fares; a red stripe means long distance.
Trains run from Tunis to Sousse, Monastir and Sfax; allow for delays. In Tunis, the TGM light railway goes to La Goulette, Carthage, Sidi Bou Said and La Marsa.
Driving is on the right. Bring your licence and an international permit, and expect police checkpoints.
Avoid driving at night: poor lighting, animals on the road and unmarked speed bumps.
Customs
Beachwear is fine at the resorts; cover up in towns, at religious sites and in the more conservative south.
Most working mosques are closed to non-Muslims; the courtyards of the Great Mosques of Kairouan, Sousse and Mahdia can be visited. Mind prayer times, above all on Friday at noon.
Do not photograph police, military or government buildings, and ask before photographing people.
Bargaining is normal in the souks; state craft shops have fixed prices, a useful guide. A tip of about 10% is usual in restaurants.
Shops do not sell alcohol on Fridays or during Ramadan; licensed hotels and bars still serve it.
Time, holidays and Ramadan
GMT+1 all year, with no summer time.
Ramadan 2027 is expected from about 8 February to 8 March, depending on the moon. Many restaurants open only at sunset; do not eat, drink or smoke in public by day.
Public holidays: 1 January, 20 March, 9 April, 1 May, 25 July, 13 August, 15 October and 17 December, plus the two Eids, the Islamic New Year and the Prophet’s birthday.
Language
Arabic is the official language; people speak Tunisian Arabic, called Tounsi or Derja.
French is widely spoken and most signs are in Arabic and French. English is common in hotels and tourist places, less elsewhere.
src/content/places.ts: Kerkouane
A Punic town on the cliffs of Cap Bon, abandoned around 250 BCE and never built over by the Romans. Its streets, houses and pink-plastered baths show how Carthaginians lived.
Ribat of Monastir
A fortress-monastery founded in 796 to guard the coast, often called the oldest ribat in North Africa. Climb the watchtower for the view over the sea and the Bourguiba mausoleum.
The capital the Fatimids founded in 916 on a narrow peninsula. You enter the old town through the Skifa el Kahla, a dark fortified gate, and end at the marine cemetery above the sea.
A hill town of the north-west, ancient Sicca Veneria, crowned by an Ottoman kasbah. Its lanes hold a Roman-era basilica, old zaouias and wide views over the high plains.
Testour
A town rebuilt in the early 17th century by Muslims expelled from Spain. The Great Mosque’s minaret carries a clock whose numbers run backwards, and its tiled roofs recall Andalusia.
Water Temple of Zaghouan
A Roman sanctuary of the 2nd century at the foot of Jebel Zaghouan, built over the spring that fed Carthage. From here an aqueduct ran about 130 km to the city.
Thuburbo Majus
A Roman town in farmland an hour from Tunis: a forum with the columns of its Capitol still standing, baths with mosaic floors and a colonnaded exercise court.
Oudhna (Uthina)
A quiet Roman site half an hour south of Tunis, with an amphitheatre dug into a hill, a huge Capitol on vaulted basements and large public baths.
Makthar
A Numidian then Roman town on a high plateau: a triumphal arch to Trajan, great baths with walls still several storeys tall, and megalithic tombs older than Rome’s rule.
Bardo Museum
One of the world’s great collections of Roman mosaics, shown in a palace of the beys in Tunis. It holds floors lifted from Carthage, Dougga, El Jem and many other Roman sites.
Chenini
A Berber village clinging to a ridge near Tataouine: cave houses cut into the rock, a ruined hilltop granary and a white mosque below the crest.
Chemtou
The quarries of the yellow “Numidian marble” that Rome shipped across its empire, with a site museum near the quarries and the remains of a Roman bridge over the Medjerda.
Tunisia’s best-known resort: long sandy beaches on a sheltered gulf, and a small walled medina with a kasbah right on the water. Jasmine bouquets are sold in the streets on summer evenings.
Mahdia’s beaches

North of the old town, a long beach of fine white sand runs past the hotel zone, with clear, shallow turquoise water. It is often ranked among the finest beaches in Tunisia, and quieter than Hammamet or Sousse.
A fishing port on Cap Bon below a hilltop fortress. The beaches of El Mansoura, a few minutes north, have white sand and very clear water.
Where the green Kroumirie mountains meet the sea. A Genoese fort crowns its former island, rock needles rise by the harbour, and its red coral beds draw divers.
Ghar El Melh
An old corsair harbour with three Ottoman forts on a lagoon. Beyond it, the beach of Sidi Ali El Mekki runs under a cape, with straw huts set up along the water’s edge in summer.
Raf Raf
A long crescent of sand below hills of vineyards, facing the rocky islet of Pilau. A popular summer beach for families from Tunis and Bizerte.
La Marsa
The seaside end of the TGM line from Tunis: a corniche, a town beach and cafés. An easy swim after a day in Carthage and Sidi Bou Said next door.
Port El Kantaoui
A marina resort built in 1979 just north of Sousse, in the white-and-blue style of the coast: boat trips, a golf course and hotel beaches on either side.
Kerkennah Islands
Flat, quiet islands an hour by ferry from Sfax, ringed by shallow turquoise water. Fishermen still use the charfia, fences of palm fronds set in the sea, listed by UNESCO as living heritage.
Djerba’s beaches
The island’s north-east coast is one long beach of fine sand, from Sidi Mahrez to Seguia, with warm shallow water from late spring well into autumn.
A southern coast of white sand and palms, backed by vast olive groves. Calmer than Djerba, which you reach by a causeway on Roman foundations to the north.
Korbous
A spa village squeezed between cliffs and sea on Cap Bon, known since Roman times for its hot springs. At Aïn Atrous the hot water pours straight into the sea, and people bathe where they mix.
Ichkeul National Park

A lake and marshes under a lone mountain, and a major stopover for hundreds of thousands of migrating birds: ducks, geese, storks and flamingos, many of which winter on the lake. World Heritage since 1980.
A mountain village with red-tiled roofs at about 800 m in the Kroumirie, the wettest corner of Tunisia. Forests of cork oak all around, mist in autumn and often snow in winter.
El Haouaria
The tip of Cap Bon, facing Sicily. Sea caves that were Punic and Roman stone quarries, a town of falconers with a festival each June, and birds of prey crossing the strait in spring.
Cape Angela
Officially the northernmost point of Africa, a rocky cape west of Bizerte marked by a monument shaped like the map of Africa.
Jebel Chambi
Tunisia’s highest mountain, 1,544 m, above Kasserine, covered in Aleppo pine. It is a national park, but it has been a closed military zone since 2014 and is not open to visitors.
Bou Hedma National Park
A last piece of acacia savanna on the steppes north of the Sahara. Scimitar-horned oryx, brought back here in 1985, graze under the trees with ostriches.
Zembra
A steep island in the Gulf of Tunis, held by the army and protected as a national park with huge seabird colonies. Landing needs a permit, but you see it from much of Cap Bon’s coast.
Jugurtha’s Table
A flat-topped mountain with sheer sides, 1,271 m high, near the Algerian border. Steps cut in the rock lead to the top, where the Numidian king Jugurtha is said to have held out against Rome.

The capital of the Djerid, beside a palm grove of hundreds of thousands of date palms. In the old quarter of Ouled el Hadef, walls of pale brick are laid in geometric patterns found almost only here and in Nefta.
Nefta
An oasis town of domes and Sufi shrines near the Algerian border. Its “Corbeille” is a deep natural bowl filled with palms, seen from the cafés on its rim.
Chebika
A mountain oasis at the mouth of a gorge: a spring, a small waterfall and palms below bare rock. The old village above was left after the floods of 1969.
Tamerza
The largest of the mountain oases, with waterfalls in a canyon and, across the dry riverbed, the empty mud-brick village abandoned after the 1969 floods.
Midès
An old village on the lip of a winding canyon, almost on the Algerian border. The layered walls of the gorge drop straight from the last houses.
The largest salt lake of the Sahara, mostly dry in summer. A causeway road crosses its white crust between Tozeur and Kebili, with pools of pink and green brine and mirages on the horizon.

The “gateway to the Sahara”: a palm-grove town on the edge of the dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental. Camel treks start here, and each winter the Festival of the Sahara fills the town with riders and poets.
Ksar Ghilane
A small oasis with a warm spring pool, right where the great dunes begin. At sunset you can walk or ride across the sand to the ruin of a Roman frontier fort.
Ong Jemel and Mos Espa
A rock shaped like a camel’s neck above the desert plain north of Nefta. Nearby stands the town of Mos Espa, built in 1997 as a set for Star Wars and left in the desert.
Selja Gorges and the Red Lizard

A deep red canyon north-west of Metlaoui. The Lézard Rouge, a train of early 20th-century carriages once used by the bey, runs through it; its service has stopped and restarted over the years, so check before you go.
March to June, September to November
June to September
March to May; winter for the birds
October to April
Roman Africa
From Carthage to the amphitheatre of El Jem through the cities of the grain lands.
Medinas and ribats
The old Islamic cities, from the souks of Tunis to the Fatimid peninsula of Mahdia.
The northern coast and Cap Bon
Coral coast, the tip of Africa, lagoon beaches and the capes facing Sicily.
Oases and the great dunes
Palm groves, mountain oases, the salt lake and a night by the dunes.
The Star Wars trail
Film locations of Tatooine: Ajim on Djerba, the Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata, the salt lake and the Mos Espa set.

src/sites/bulla-regia.ts: House of the Hunt

Its underground floor is a courtyard lit by a light well, with Corinthian columns carrying stone architraves. Wealthy families of Bulla Regia dug such floors to escape the summer heat of the plain. The house is named after a hunting mosaic on its upper floor.
House of Amphitrite

Its underground room holds the most famous mosaic of the site: Venus carried over the sea by two sea-centaurs, long taken for the sea-goddess Amphitrite, hence the name. The floor here is a generated pattern; the photo shows the real mosaic, still in place.
House of the Fishing
Thought to be the earliest of the underground houses. Beside a fountain in its basement, a small room has a mosaic of fishermen at work among fish and sea creatures.
The theatre

Built under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (161–169 CE), on flat ground with its seats carried on vaults. A 4th-century mosaic of a bear lies in the orchestra. Around 399 Saint Augustine preached here, scolding the townspeople for their love of the shows.
The forum

The paved square at the heart of the town, with the Temple of Apollo on one side and the Capitol on another. Bulla Regia was a royal city of the Numidian kings, hence its name, before it became Roman.
Baths of Julia Memmia
The largest baths of the town, near the entrance, where high walls and arches of the halls still stand.
The Byzantine fort
In the 6th century, when the town had shrunk, the Byzantines built a small fort here from the stones of older buildings.
Known for
houses with underground floors
Before Rome
a royal city of the Numidian kings
Theatre
at the foot of Jebel Rebia, near Jendouba
About 6 km north of Jendouba; louages and taxis run from Jendouba, which has trains and buses from Tunis.
An entry fee; the small museum is at the entrance. Bring a torch for the underground rooms.
Spring, when the plain is green; in summer, do as the Romans did and go underground at midday.
A Roman town whose rich houses had a second floor under the ground: walk down into their columned courtyards and mosaic rooms.
Digging out the villas of Bulla Regia…
Terrain, paths and the outline of every ruin come from real map data; the underground floors are modelled from photos and simplified, and the mosaics are generated patterns.
src/sites/carthage.ts: The frigidarium column

The great cold hall stood on eight granite columns about 15 m tall, brought from Egypt. One was raised again in the 20th century with a marble capital: it shows how high the vaults once rose above the floor you walk on.
The service level
What survives is the basement: vaulted rooms where slaves fed the furnaces and water flowed to the pools above. The bathing halls themselves, one of the largest in the Roman world, have vanished.
Hot rooms facing the sea

Built between 145 and 162 CE under Antoninus Pius, the baths were symmetrical along an axis running to the sea. The hot rooms, the caldaria, opened onto the gulf in great apses to catch the afternoon sun.
The latrines
A horseshoe of stone seats where bathers sat side by side and talked; water ran in a channel beneath. They are among the best-preserved parts of the complex.
The Roman theatre
Built in the 2nd century and heavily restored, the theatre is cut into the hillside. Every summer it hosts the International Festival of Carthage, one of the oldest festivals in Africa.
Villa of the Aviary
On the hill of the Roman villas, a rich house with a colonnaded garden court, named after a mosaic of birds. Its portico was partly rebuilt to show how such houses looked.
Byrsa and the Saint-Louis cathedral

Byrsa was the citadel of Punic Carthage, where legend says Queen Dido founded the city in 814 BCE. The cathedral was built on the summit in 1890; it is now a cultural venue, next to the National Museum of Carthage.
The Punic quarter
On the slope of Byrsa, the houses of Hannibal’s time: narrow streets, cisterns and walls with the earth fill the Romans dumped on them in 146 BCE when they levelled the hill.
Founded
814 BCE (tradition), by Phoenicians
Destroyed
by Rome in 146 BCE, rebuilt as a Roman city
Antonine Baths
145–162 CE, about 200 m along the sea
TGM light railway from Tunis Marine: Carthage Hannibal for the Antonine Baths, Carthage Byrsa for the hill and the museum.
One ticket usually covers several sites (baths, Byrsa and museum, theatre, villas, Punic ports, Tophet). Check current prices and hours.
Spring and autumn mornings. The sites are spread over several kilometres: combine with Sidi Bou Said, one stop further.
From Byrsa Hill to the sea: the Antonine Baths, the Roman theatre and the Punic quarter, on the real terrain and streets.
Raising the columns of Carthage…

src/sites/djerba.ts: By tradition the oldest synagogue in Africa, founded by priests who fled Jerusalem after the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE. The present building dates mostly from the late 19th century. Every spring, for Lag BaOmer, pilgrims come from Tunisia and abroad.

Walls of blue tiles, white arches on blue columns, a painted wooden ceiling and brass lamps. Visitors take off their shoes and cover their heads; the Torah scrolls are kept in the Ark at the end of the hall.
Beside the synagogue, a large guesthouse with two storeys of rooms round a courtyard, built to lodge the pilgrims who come for the annual festival.

In 2014 about 150 street artists from some 30 countries painted the walls of Erriadh, turning the old village of Hara Sghira into an open-air gallery. The murals here are generated, in the spirit of the real ones.
The island has hundreds of small mosques, many of the Ibadi tradition: white, thick-walled and sometimes fortified, with short minarets, once used as lookouts against raiders from the sea.

Instead of large villages, Djerbians long lived in scattered family estates: white houses with vaulted and domed rooms round a courtyard, a cistern for rainwater, and palms and olive trees around. This way of settling the island is why Djerba was listed by UNESCO in 2023.
Small white domed shrines such as Sidi Salama El Jenaouni stand among the fields, tombs of holy men visited by the people of the island.
about 514 km², the largest in North Africa
Fly to Djerba-Zarzis, or drive over the causeway from Zarzis or take the ferry from Jorf to Ajim. Erriadh is about 7 km south of Houmt Souk.
A small fee for the Ghriba; dress modestly, cover your head and take off your shoes. The murals of Erriadh are free to see.
Morning or late afternoon; the pilgrimage in spring is lively but crowded and closely guarded.
The Ghriba synagogue, the painted village of Erriadh and the island’s white houses among palms and olive trees, on the real streets.
Terrain, streets and every house outline come from real map data; the Ghriba is modelled from photos and simplified, and the murals are generated.
src/sites/dougga.ts: The Capitol

Dedicated in 166–167 CE to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva for the health of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Its porch of Corinthian columns and pediment still stand to almost full height, the emblem of Dougga.
Square of the Winds

A paved square beside the forum, named after the compass rose carved into its slabs: a circle with the names of twelve winds, such as Septentrio, Africus and Aquilo. Merchants and citizens met here between the temples.

Built in 168–169 CE by a rich citizen, Publius Marcius Quadratus, for about 3,500 spectators. The seats are cut into the hillside and the stage looks over the valley; every summer it hosts a festival of classical theatre.
Temple of Juno Caelestis

Built under Severus Alexander (222–235 CE) for Caelestis, the Roman form of the Punic goddess Tanit. The temple stands in a half-moon court lined with columns, a shape that recalls the crescent of the goddess.
The Libyco-Punic mausoleum

A tower tomb of the 2nd century BCE, about 21 m tall, from the time of the Numidian kings. Its bilingual inscription in Libyc and Punic was cut out in 1842 and is now in the British Museum; the monument was rebuilt from its fallen stones in 1908–1910.
Arch of Severus Alexander
A single-bay arch at the western edge of town, raised in the 3rd century in honour of the emperor Severus Alexander. Another arch, for Septimius Severus, marks the road to Carthage on the east side.
The Licinian Baths
Winter baths of the 3rd century, paid for by the Licinii family. Their walls stand high, and a long vaulted service corridor still runs beneath the halls where slaves stoked the furnaces.
Temple of Saturn
Built in 195 CE at the north-east edge of the town, over an older sanctuary of the Punic god Baal Hammon. A few columns of its porch stand against the sky above the valley.
Ancient name
Thugga, a Numidian then Roman town
Area
about 70 ha on a hillside at 570 m
Capitol
World Heritage since 1997
About 110 km south-west of Tunis, near Téboursouk (Béja governorate). By car, or louage to Téboursouk and a taxi for the last few kilometres.
Pay at the entrance. The site is large and hilly: allow at least three hours. Check current prices and hours.
Spring, when the fields are green and flowers grow among the stones. There is little shade: bring water and good shoes.
A whole Roman town on its hillside: the Capitol, the theatre, temples, baths and a Numidian mausoleum, on the real terrain.
Climbing the hill of Thugga…

src/sites/el-jem.ts: A reconstruction of the amphitheatre as it stands today, built to its real dimensions.
Procedural reconstruction for illustration, based on published dimensions and reference photos. Details are simplified.
src/sites/kairouan.ts: The minaret

Built in the early 9th century, about 31.5 m tall in three tiers, it is one of the oldest standing minarets in the world. Its square, battered shape became the model for minarets across North Africa and Andalusia.
The courtyard

A vast marble-paved court ringed by arcades of horseshoe arches. It slopes gently towards the centre, where rainwater drains into a great cistern below; the carved well-heads drew it up. A sundial gave the hours of prayer.
The prayer hall

Seventeen naves on hundreds of marble and granite columns, many reused from Roman and Byzantine buildings such as those of Carthage. At the end of the wider central nave, the mihrab is lined with 9th-century lustre tiles from Baghdad, beside the oldest minbar in the Islamic world still in place.
The Aghlabid basins

Built around 862 to store water brought by aqueduct for a city on a dry plain. The large basin, about 128 m across with rounded buttresses all round, held a pavilion on its central pier where the emir could rest.
Mausoleum of Sidi Sahab

The shrine of Abu Zama al-Balawi, a companion of the Prophet, known as "the Barber" because he is said to have kept three hairs of the Prophet’s beard. The 17th-century courts are lined with tiles and carved stucco.
Mosque of the Three Doors

Founded in 866 by Muhammad ibn Khayrun, from Andalusia. Its carved façade, with three arched doors and bands of Kufic inscriptions and floral friezes, is one of the oldest decorated mosque façades in Islamic art.
Bir Barouta

A well dug, by tradition, in the 17th century, in a domed building. Upstairs a blindfolded camel still walks in circles to turn the wheel that raises the water. Legend says it is linked to the well of Zamzam in Mecca.
The ramparts and Bab ech Chouhada
About 3 km of brick ramparts with bastions enclose the medina; most date from the 18th century, on older lines. Bab ech Chouhada, the Gate of the Martyrs, is the main way in from the south.
670 CE, by Uqba ibn Nafi
Great Mosque
rebuilt 836 under the Aghlabids, about 9,000 m²
Medina
about 54 ha inside 3 km of ramparts
World Heritage since 1988
About 2 h by road from Tunis, 1 h from Sousse; buses and louages arrive at the station west of the medina.

A combined ticket covers the Great Mosque, the Aghlabid basins and other monuments. Non-Muslim visitors see the prayer hall from its doors; the mosque closes to visitors at prayer times and on Friday afternoons. Dress modestly.
Spring and autumn mornings; summers on the plain are very hot. Try the makroudh, date pastries for which Kairouan is famous.
The Great Mosque of Uqba, the walled medina and the Aghlabid basins, on the real streets of Kairouan.

src/sites/ksar-ouled-soltane.ts: The second courtyard

In the 19th century the ksar was extended with a second courtyard, bringing it to around 400 ghorfas. The tribes of the plain kept their harvests here, safe from raids, and came back to fetch grain and oil as they needed them.
The first courtyard

The oldest part of the ksar, often dated to the 15th century (some historians say 1699): vaulted ghorfas stacked four storeys high around a closed courtyard. In 1997 it was filmed for Star Wars: The Phantom Menace.
Inside a ghorfa

Each ghorfa is a long barrel-vaulted cell of stone and mud plaster, with a small wooden door. Thick walls kept grain, oil and dried food cool and dry through the summer; each family had its own cells.
Stairs without railings
Narrow stair ramps of plastered stone climb the walls to the upper doors. Beam ends sticking out under the doors served as footholds and to hoist sacks up by rope.
Between the two courtyards
A short passage, roofed with palm trunks, joins the two courtyards.
On the hilltop
From outside the ksar shows almost blank walls: a fortress of granaries on a hilltop of the Dahar, about 20 km south of Tataouine, above the village that took its name.
first courtyard 15th c. (or 1699), second 19th c.
Ghorfas
about 400, up to four storeys
Use
fortified granary of grain and olive oil
Altitude
about 500 m, in the Dahar hills
About 20 km south of Tataouine by a winding road; take a taxi or join a tour of the ksour.
Free to walk in; there is a café by the entrance. Take care on the stairs, which have no railings.
Early morning or late afternoon, when the low sun warms the ochre walls; spring and autumn are the most comfortable.
A fortified granary on a hilltop of the south: two courtyards ringed by vaulted cells stacked four storeys high.
Stacking the ghorfas…

src/sites/matmata.ts: Hotel Sidi Driss

A family house of several courtyard pits joined by underground passages, now a hotel. In 1976 this courtyard was filmed as the home of Luke Skywalker in Star Wars, which made Matmata known around the world.
A room in the rock

Vaulted rooms are dug into the soft rock all round the courtyard and lime-washed inside. Under several metres of earth they stay cool in the summer heat and mild on winter nights. The upper openings are granaries for grain and oil.
The entrance tunnel

The only way in is a sloping tunnel, the sqifa, dug from the hillside down to the courtyard. A sunken lane leads to its whitewashed mouth; inside, it was also a place to keep animals and to receive visitors.
Dar Khadija

A troglodyte house kept as a small museum, furnished as a Berber family lived in it, with the tools of daily life in the rooms round the courtyard. Several families often shared one house, each with its own rooms.
An abandoned courtyard

In 1969 weeks of rain soaked the soft rock and many pits collapsed. Many families moved to New Matmata, built on the plain to the north, and many courtyards have stood empty since. (This pit is generated, among the mapped ones.)
A village of craters

Seen from the hills, Matmata is a field of round holes. Its Berber people dug their houses into the soft rock of the Dahar hills, sheltered from the heat and wind, with olive trees and palms in the hollows where the rain water gathers behind small earth dams (jessour).
The village above ground
The mosque, the shops and the newer stone houses of Matmata stand above ground, on the hill around which the pits are dug. Some families still live in their courtyards; others open them to visitors.
Houses
courtyards dug 6 to 9 m deep, with rooms in their walls
People
Berber (Amazigh)
Matmata el Qadima and Hotel Sidi Driss
about 400 m, in the Dahar hills
About 45 km south-west of Gabès by road, through New Matmata; louages (shared taxis) run from Gabès.
Small fees for Hotel Sidi Driss and Dar Khadija; some families show their homes for a tip.
Spring and autumn; in summer the courtyards are the coolest place to be at midday.
The pit houses of a Berber village, dug into the hills: walk down the tunnels into their courtyards and rooms.

src/sites/sbeitla.ts: The three temples

Instead of a single Capitol, Sufetula built three separate temples side by side in the 2nd century, for Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, linked by arches. They are among the best-preserved Roman temples in North Africa.
The Antonine gate

The monumental entrance to the forum, a gate of three arches dedicated in 139 CE to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons. Through it, the three temples appear framed at the end of the square.
Arch of the Tetrarchy
A triumphal arch of about 300 CE, at the southern entrance of the town, dedicated to the four emperors who then shared the empire, Diocletian and Maximian with their deputies.
Built on the bank of the wadi, with the river behind the stage. Some columns of the stage front have been raised again; the theatre hosts the Sbeitla spring festival.
Church of Vitalis
A large Christian basilica of the 5th–6th century with five aisles. Its baptistery keeps a baptismal font lined with bright mosaics of crosses, fish and candles.
Church of Bellator
One of the great churches of the town centre, named after Bellator, who appears in an inscription. Its columns still mark the nave and aisles; beside it stands the small chapel of Bishop Jucundus.
The great baths
Public baths with cold, warm and hot rooms, a palaestra for exercise, and floors on small brick pillars so that hot air from the furnaces could run underneath.
The Byzantine forts

In the 6th and 7th centuries, the Byzantines turned houses and buildings of the old town into small forts. In 647 the first Arab army defeated the exarch Gregory near Sufetula, the start of the Muslim conquest of Ifriqiya.
Sufetula, founded in the 1st century
Forum temples
2nd century CE
Battle
647, Arab victory over the Byzantines
about 540 m, on the steppe of central Tunisia
In Kasserine governorate, about 1 h 30 west of Kairouan by road; the site is at the northern edge of the modern town.
One ticket for the site and its small museum near the entrance. Check current prices and hours.
Late afternoon, when the low sun warms the temples’ stone; spring and autumn. Allow two to three hours.
The forum and its three temples, the triumphal arches, the theatre and the Byzantine churches of Sufetula, on the real terrain.

src/sites/sidi-bou-said.ts: At the top of a broad flight of steps, the oldest café of the village takes its name from the straw mats (nattes) its regulars sat on. Painters and writers from Paul Klee to Simone de Beauvoir stopped here.
The village grew around the zaouia of Abu Said al-Baji, a Sufi teacher who died here in 1231. His sanctuary and the white minaret still crown the hill and gave Sidi Bou Said its name.

In 1915 Baron Rodolphe d’Erlanger had the village protected: walls stay lime-washed white, doors, shutters and window grilles painted blue. The studded doors carry patterns of black nails that once told who lived inside.
On the summit of the cape, about 130 m above the sea, the lighthouse guides ships into the Gulf of Tunis. The hill was a lookout long before: ancient sailors called the cape Promontorium Apollinis.
From the cliff the view runs across the gulf to the twin peaks of Bou Kornine and the Cap Bon peninsula. The cafés on the terraces below are the classic place to watch the sun set over the water.

Officially the Café Sidi Chabaane, its white terraces step down the cliff towards the marina, with blue-and-white benches under blue umbrellas. It is the classic place for mint tea with pine nuts at sunset.
Built from 1912 to 1922 by Baron d’Erlanger, a musicologist who loved Arab music, this palace mixes Andalusian and Tunisian crafts. It now houses the Centre of Arab and Mediterranean Music.
Below the cliff, sailing boats and fishing boats share the small harbour. A path and steps lead down from the village; the walk back up is steep but worth the view.
Take the TGM light railway from Tunis Marine to the Sidi Bou Said stop (about 35 minutes), then walk up the main street.
Early morning before the crowds, or late afternoon for the sunset over the gulf. Spring brings the bougainvillea and jasmine.
The ruins of Carthage are one TGM stop away; La Marsa and its beach are next door.
The village on its cliff above the Gulf of Tunis, built on the real terrain, streets and houses.
Terrain, streets and many buildings come from real map data; houses on unmapped plots and all details are generated from reference photos.
src/sites/sousse.ts: The Ribat

A fortified monastery of the late 8th century, finished in 821: warrior-monks lived in its cells, prayed and watched the sea for Byzantine ships. It is one of the oldest and best preserved ribats of the North African coast.
Inside the Ribat

Two storeys of cells round a courtyard, with the prayer hall upstairs on the south side. The round watchtower, the nador, rises about 27 m; from its top, fire and smoke signals could be passed along a chain of ribats down the coast.
The Great Mosque

Built in 850–851 under the Aghlabid emir Abu al-Abbas Muhammad, next to the Ribat. With its crenellated walls and corner towers it looks like a fortress; it has no minaret, and the call to prayer was given from the small domed kiosk on a tower. A band of Kufic inscription runs above the courtyard arches.
The Kasbah and the Khalef al-Fata tower
On the highest corner of the medina, the Kasbah guards the town. Its square tower, built in 859 and about 30 m tall, has served as a lighthouse for ships coming into Sousse.
The Archaeological Museum

Inside the Kasbah, around garden courts, one of the finest collections of Roman mosaics after the Bardo in Tunis: sea gods, Bacchus and hunting scenes from Hadrumetum, as Sousse was called in Roman times.
The Kalaout el-Koubba

A medieval hall known for its dome with zigzag ribs, a design found nowhere else in Tunisia. Probably built in the 11th century, it may have been a meeting place or a tomb; today it houses a museum of traditional arts and costumes.
The souks
Covered and open lanes of shops cross the medina from Bab el Gharbi towards the Great Mosque: spices, leather, copper, carpets and jewellery, as in the souks of every Tunisian medina.
The ramparts
About 2.25 km of 9th-century walls still surround the medina, among the best preserved in the Islamic world. Bab el Gharbi, the western gate, leads into the souks.
Hadrumetum, a Phoenician then Roman port
Ribat
completed 821
850–851, Aghlabid
About 2 h by train or road from Tunis; Sousse Bab Jedid station is at the foot of the medina walls, by the harbour.
Separate tickets for the Ribat, the Great Mosque courtyard and the Archaeological Museum. The mosque closes to visitors at prayer times. Check current prices and hours.
Morning, before the heat and the crowds; climb the Ribat’s tower for the view over the medina and the sea.
The Ribat, the Great Mosque, the Kasbah and the walled medina above the harbour, on the real streets of Sousse.
Manning the walls of Sousse…

src/sites/tunis-medina.ts: The Zitouna Mosque

The great mosque at the heart of the medina, around which the city grew. Founded in the early 8th century and rebuilt under the Aghlabids in the 9th, its prayer hall has 15 naves on about 160 ancient columns, many taken from Carthage. The 43 m minaret was built in 1894 on the model of the Kasbah Mosque’s. For centuries the mosque was also one of the great universities of the Islamic world.
Souk el Attarine

The perfumers’ souk, laid out around 1240 under the Hafsid ruler Abu Zakariya beside the Zitouna, is the oldest in Tunis. Under its vaults, shops sell essences of jasmine and rose, amber, henna and incense. The trades were arranged round the mosque: perfumes, books and fine cloth close by, noisier crafts such as the dyers and the blacksmiths further out.
The Kasbah Mosque

Built from about 1230 for Abu Zakariya, founder of the Hafsid dynasty, inside the citadel (kasbah) that stood here. Its minaret, finished in 1233, with panels of lozenge-net decoration in pale stone, follows the Almohad style of Marrakesh and became the model for the Zitouna’s. The square beside it is lined with ministries and the Prime Minister’s offices in Dar el Bey.
Youssef Dey Mosque

Finished around 1615 for Youssef Dey, it was the first mosque in Tunis built by the Ottoman rulers, for the Hanafi rite of the Turks. Its octagonal minaret, the first in the city, set the pattern for the Ottoman mosques that followed.
Hammouda Pacha Mosque
Built in 1655 by Hammouda Pacha Bey, it was the second Hanafi mosque in Tunis. Its slender octagonal minaret follows the model of the Youssef Dey Mosque.
Tourbet el Bey

The largest mausoleum in Tunis, built under Ali II Bey (r. 1759–1782) for the Husainid beys, who ruled Tunisia until 1957. Most of the dynasty’s rulers lie here, in chambers under domes covered with green, scale-shaped tiles. Nearby stands Dar Ben Abdallah, an 18th-century palace that is now a museum of traditional life.
Sidi Mahrez Mosque

Begun in 1692 by Mohamed Bey el Mouradi, opposite the tomb of Sidi Mahrez, patron saint of Tunis. Unlike the other mosques of the city, it follows the great Ottoman mosques of Istanbul: a central dome with smaller domes round it, and no minaret. Its walls are lined with tiles from Iznik in Turkey.
Bab Bhar

The Sea Gate, also called the Porte de France, stands where the medina meets the new town built from the late 19th century towards the lake. From here the Rue Jamaa Zitouna climbs through the souks to the Great Mosque.
Heart
the Zitouna Mosque, founded in the 8th century
Capital
of the Hafsids from 1229, then of the Ottoman deys and the beys
Monuments
some 700: mosques, palaces, mausoleums, madrasas, fountains
In central Tunis: walk from the Avenue Habib Bourguiba through Bab Bhar, then up the Rue Jamaa Zitouna.
The lanes and souks are free. Non-Muslim visitors may look into the Zitouna’s courtyard from the visitors’ area outside prayer times; dress modestly. Some palaces are museums with tickets.
Mornings, when the souks open. Climb to a rooftop café for the view over the minarets.
The Zitouna Mosque, the vaulted souks, the minarets and the gates, on the real lanes of the medina of Tunis.
Opening the souks of Tunis…
